Let <MATH_0001> be a Noetherian scheme. Let <MATH_0002> be a quasi-compact unramified
morphism. Let <MATH_0003> be a morphism with <MATH_0004> Noetherian. Then
<MATH_0005> is a finite set.

Assume first <MATH_0001> is separated (which is often the case in practice).
Since <MATH_0002> is Noetherian it has finitely many connected components. Thus we
may assume <MATH_0003> is connected. Choose a point <MATH_0004> with image <MATH_0005>.
Since <MATH_0006> is unramified and quasi-compact
then fibre <MATH_0007> is finite, say <MATH_0008>
and <MATH_0009> is a finite field extension.
See Morphisms, Lemma <REF_0001>,
<REF_0002>, and
<REF_0003>.
For each <MATH_0010> there are at most finitely many <MATH_0011>-algebra
maps <MATH_0012> (by elementary field theory).
Thus <MATH_0013> is finite by
Proposition <REF_0004>.

General case. There exists a nonempty open <MATH_0014> such
that <MATH_0015> is finite (in particular separated), see
Morphisms, Lemma <REF_0005>
(the lemma applies since we've already seen above that a quasi-compact
unramified morphism is quasi-finite and since <MATH_0016> is quasi-separated by
Morphisms, Lemma <REF_0006>).
Let <MATH_0017> be the reduced closed subscheme supported on
the complement of <MATH_0018>. By Noetherian induction, we see that
<MATH_0019> is finite (details omitted).
By the result of the first paragraph the set
<MATH_0020> is finite. Thus it suffices to show that
<MATH_0021>
is injective. This follows from the fact that the set of points where
two morphisms <MATH_0022> agree is open in <MATH_0023>, due to the fact
that <MATH_0024> is open, see
Morphisms, Lemma <REF_0007>.
